notes.front: What is the Cilium CLI (`cilium`)?
notes.back: A command-line tool to install Cilium, inspect the state of an installation, and enable or disable features such as Hubble.
notes.explanation: It runs on your own machine against the cluster, unlike the Cilium debug CLI, which runs inside an agent pod.
notes.example: Like `kubectl`, but its commands (`cilium install`, `cilium status`) speak about the Cilium installation as a whole.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Cilium Quick Installation”, “Install the Cilium CLI”
notes.evidence: The Cilium CLI can be used to install Cilium, inspect the state of a Cilium installation, and enable/disable various features (e.g. clustermesh, Hubble).

notes.front: What is the `cilium-config` ConfigMap?
notes.back: The shared ConfigMap holding the arguments of Cilium's components, stored without the leading `--`.
notes.explanation: The installation's Helm values end up here as component arguments.
notes.example: Like a settings file for the agent, such as `auto-direct-node-routes: "false"`, but kept as a ConfigMap in the cluster.
notes.evidence: These arguments are stored in a shared ConfigMap called cilium-config (albeit without the leading --).

notes.front: What is a CiliumNodeConfig object for?
notes.back: Applying Cilium configuration to a set of nodes rather than the whole cluster.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three documented ways to change a running installation.
notes.example: Like a local by-law that applies only in some districts, while the national law (`cilium-config`) covers everyone.
notes.evidence: Via CiliumNodeConfig objects Cilium also supports configuration on sets of nodes.

notes.front: What does the quick installation with `cilium install` choose for you, and where does it keep state?
notes.back: It detects and uses the best configuration for your Kubernetes distribution, and stores all state in CRDs.
notes.explanation: The docs call it the best installation method for most use cases.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Cilium Quick Installation”, “Cilium Quick Installation”
notes.evidence: It will automatically detect and use the best configuration possible for the Kubernetes distribution you are using. All state is stored using Kubernetes custom resource definitions (CRDs).

notes.front: Into which cluster does `cilium install` install Cilium?
notes.back: The cluster that your current `kubectl` context points to.
notes.explanation: The command follows the same context as `kubectl`, so check the context before installing.
notes.evidence: Install Cilium into the Kubernetes cluster pointed to by your current kubectl context:

notes.front: Which two requirements does the generic quick installation list?
notes.back: Kubernetes configured to use CNI, and Linux kernel 5.10 or newer.
notes.explanation: These appear as the requirements of the generic install tab; platform tabs add their own.
notes.evidence: Requirements: Kubernetes must be configured to use CNI (see Network Plugin Requirements) Linux kernel >= 5.10

notes.front: Why might `cilium install` print lines such as "Restarted unmanaged pod"?
notes.back: Pods were running before Cilium, so the installer restarted them to give them Cilium networking.
notes.explanation: Pods started before Cilium are not managed by it until they restart.
notes.evidence: This indicates that your cluster was already running some pods before Cilium was deployed and the installer has automatically restarted them to ensure all pods get networking provided by Cilium.

notes.front: Which command validates that Cilium has been properly installed?
notes.back: `cilium status --wait`.
notes.explanation: It reports the agent, Operator, Hubble and Cluster Mesh states and waits for them to be ready.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Cilium Quick Installation”, “Validate the Installation”
notes.evidence: To validate that Cilium has been properly installed, you can run $ cilium status --wait

notes.front: What should you do first if `cilium install` fails?
notes.back: Run `cilium status` for the overall state, then inspect the logs of the pods that fail to deploy.
notes.explanation: The status output shows which component is not ready.
notes.evidence: If the installation fails for some reason, run cilium status to retrieve the overall status of the Cilium deployment and inspect the logs of whatever pods are failing to be deployed.

notes.front: What does `cilium connectivity test` check?
notes.back: That the cluster has proper network connectivity, by running a set of tests and reporting the results.
notes.explanation: It creates its own namespace for the checks and ends with a test report.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Cilium Quick Installation”, “Validate the Installation”
notes.evidence: Run the following command to validate that your cluster has proper network connectivity: $ cilium connectivity test

notes.front: What can make the connectivity test fail to deploy, and what is the remedy?
notes.back: Too many open files in its pods; raise the inotify resource limits on the host.
notes.explanation: The failure comes from host limits, not from Cilium's networking.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Cilium Quick Installation”, “Validate the Installation”
notes.evidence: The connectivity test may fail to deploy due to too many open files in one or more of the pods. If you notice this error, you can increase the inotify resource limits on your host machine

notes.front: What must you decide yourself when installing Cilium with Helm rather than with the quick install?
notes.back: The best datapath and IP address management mode for your environment.
notes.explanation: The quick install picks these automatically; Helm leaves them to you.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Installation using Helm”, “Installation using Helm”
notes.evidence: This involves a couple of additional steps compared to the Cilium Quick Installation and requires you to manually select the best datapath and IPAM mode for your particular environment.

notes.front: Which Helm installation method do the docs recommend, and what does it save you?
notes.back: Installing straight from a container registry with `oci://quay.io/cilium/charts/cilium`; no `helm repo add` is needed.
notes.explanation: The traditional alternative uses the `https://helm.cilium.io/` repository, which must be added first.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Installation using Helm”, “Helm Installation Methods”
notes.evidence: OCI Registry (Recommended) — Install directly from OCI registries without adding a Helm repository Traditional Repository — Use the classic https://helm.cilium.io/ repository

notes.front: How must the Cilium version be written in Helm commands?
notes.back: Without the "v" prefix, for example `1.20.2`; image tags keep the "v".
notes.explanation: Helm chart versions follow SemVer 2.0 without the prefix.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Installation using Helm”, “Using OCI Registries (Recommended)”
notes.evidence: Helm chart versions follow SemVer 2.0 without the “v” prefix (e.g., 1.15.0). Container image tags include the “v” (e.g., v1.15.0). Use versions without the “v” for Helm commands.

notes.front: Which node taint lets a cluster avoid manually restarting unmanaged pods after installing Cilium?
notes.back: `node.cilium.io/agent-not-ready`, for example `node.cilium.io/agent-not-ready=true:NoExecute`.
notes.explanation: With the taint, application pods are only scheduled once Cilium is ready to manage them.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Installation using Helm”, “Restart unmanaged Pods”
notes.evidence: If you did not create a cluster with the nodes tainted with the taint node.cilium.io/agent-not-ready, then unmanaged pods need to be restarted manually.

notes.front: Which already-running pods must be restarted after a Helm install without the taint?
notes.back: All pods not running in host-networking mode.
notes.explanation: Restarting them gives them Cilium connectivity and makes NetworkPolicy apply to them.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Installation using Helm”, “Restart unmanaged Pods”
notes.evidence: Restart all already running pods which are not running in host-networking mode to ensure that Cilium starts managing them. This is required to ensure that all pods which have been running before Cilium was deployed have network connectivity provided by Cilium and NetworkPolicy applies to them

notes.front: What happens to the Helm values of a Cilium installation?
notes.back: They are converted into arguments for components such as cilium-agent and cilium-operator, and stored in a ConfigMap.
notes.explanation: That ConfigMap is `cilium-config`, shared by the components.
notes.evidence: These helm values are converted to arguments for the individual components of a Cilium installation, such as cilium-agent and cilium-operator, and stored in a ConfigMap.

notes.front: When changing configuration through `helm upgrade`, which value restarts the agent pods gradually?
notes.back: `rollOutCiliumPods=true`.
notes.explanation: `helm upgrade` applies new values to the existing installation; this value also rolls the agents.
notes.evidence: Via helm upgrade Do so by providing new values to Helm and applying them to the existing installation. By setting the value rollOutCiliumPods=true, the agent pods will be gradually restarted.

notes.front: What does `cilium config set` change?
notes.back: Individual values in the `cilium-config` ConfigMap.
notes.explanation: It is the Cilium CLI's route for changing a running installation, beside Helm and CiliumNodeConfig.
notes.evidence: Via cilium config set The Cilium CLI has the ability to update individual values in the cilium-config ConfigMap.

notes.front: What does `cilium config set` do to agent pods by default, and how do you restart them gradually instead?
notes.back: It restarts them; use `--restart=false`, then delete agent pods yourself.
notes.explanation: Deleting the pods one by one spreads the restarts out.
notes.evidence: By default Cilium Agent pods are restarted when configuration is changed. To gradually restart do cilium config set --restart=false ... and manually delete agent pods to pick up the changes.

notes.front: What is needed for a CiliumNodeConfig change to take effect?
notes.back: Pods must be deleted manually.
notes.explanation: Unlike `cilium config set`, it does not restart the agents for you.
notes.evidence: This requires that pods be manually deleted for changes to take effect.

notes.front: How does Cilium make visible that a running agent has not yet picked up a `cilium-config` change?
notes.back: It exposes a Prometheus metric for this drift.
notes.explanation: Many changes need an agent restart, so the running settings can lag the desired state.
notes.evidence: Because many Cilium configuration changes require an agent restart to take effect, there is a window after updating the cilium-config ConfigMap where the running agent’s settings no longer match the desired state. Cilium exposes a Prometheus metric to make this drift visible.

notes.front: How do you see the status and health of the Cilium agent on one particular node?
notes.back: Run `cilium-dbg status` inside that node's Cilium pod, for example with `kubectl exec`.
notes.explanation: `cilium status` summarises the whole installation; `cilium-dbg status` details one agent.
notes.evidence: the status and health of the agent on that node can be retrieved by running cilium-dbg status in the context of that pod:

notes.front: Which Cilium CLI command collects troubleshooting information from a cluster, and how can you limit it on a large one?
notes.back: `cilium sysdump`; on clusters above 20 nodes, use `--node-list` to pick a few nodes.
notes.explanation: By default it tries to collect as many logs as possible from all nodes.
notes.evidence: If your cluster size is above 20 nodes, consider setting the following options to limit the size of the sysdump. This is not required, but useful for those who have a constraint on bandwidth or upload size. set the --node-list option to pick only a few nodes in case the cluster has many of them.

notes.front: What does the upgrade pre-flight check do?
notes.back: It pre-pulls the new Cilium image version before the upgrade.
notes.explanation: This reduces agent downtime and prevents `ErrImagePull` errors during the upgrade.
notes.evidence: In order to reduce the downtime of the agent and to prevent ErrImagePull errors during upgrade, the pre-flight check pre-pulls the new image version.

notes.front: Between which releases are Cilium upgrades and rollbacks tested?
notes.back: Only between consecutive minor releases, one minor release at a time.
notes.explanation: So 1.1 to 1.2 and back is supported, while 1.1 to 1.3 is not.
notes.evidence: The only tested rollback and upgrade path is between consecutive minor releases. Always perform rollbacks and upgrades between one minor release at a time.

notes.front: What should you do before a minor-version upgrade of Cilium?
notes.back: Upgrade to the latest patch release of your current series.
notes.explanation: This gives the most seamless experience if a rollback is needed after the minor upgrade.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Upgrade Guide”, “Step 1: Upgrade to latest patch version”
notes.evidence: Upgrading to the latest patch release ensures the most seamless experience if a rollback is required following the minor release upgrade.

notes.front: Cilium was installed with Helm on a running cluster whose nodes had no Cilium taint. A NetworkPolicy does not seem to affect an old pod. What should you do?
notes.back: B: restart the pods that are not in host-networking mode.
notes.choices:
A) Reinstall Cilium with `cilium install`
B) Restart the pods that are not in host-networking mode
C) Delete the `cilium-config` ConfigMap
D) Run `cilium connectivity test`
notes.choicesExplained: A: a reinstall is not needed; the old pods simply are not managed yet. C: deleting the configuration breaks Cilium. D: the test checks connectivity but changes nothing.
notes.explanation: Pods started before Cilium only come under its management, and its policy, once restarted.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Installation using Helm”, “Restart unmanaged Pods”
notes.evidence: This is required to ensure that all pods which have been running before Cilium was deployed have network connectivity provided by Cilium and NetworkPolicy applies to them

notes.front: You must change one Cilium setting on a busy cluster and do not want every agent to restart at once. What fits the docs?
notes.back: B: `cilium config set --restart=false`, then delete agent pods gradually.
notes.choices:
A) `cilium config set` with no flags
B) `cilium config set --restart=false`, then delete agent pods gradually
C) `cilium connectivity test`
D) Edit a CiliumNode object
notes.choicesExplained: A: by default the agents are restarted when the value changes. D: CiliumNode is not a configuration object for agent settings. C: the test only validates connectivity.
notes.explanation: With restarts deferred, you choose when each agent picks up the change.
notes.evidence: To gradually restart do cilium config set --restart=false ... and manually delete agent pods to pick up the changes.

notes.front: `cilium status --wait` reports every component as healthy, but you want proof that pods can really reach each other. What next?
notes.back: C: `cilium connectivity test`.
notes.choices:
A) `cilium config set`
B) `cilium sysdump`
C) `cilium connectivity test`
D) `helm repo add cilium`
notes.choicesExplained: B: sysdump collects logs for troubleshooting. A: this changes configuration. D: this adds a chart repository.
notes.explanation: The status only shows the components are up; the test checks network connectivity.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Cilium Quick Installation”, “Validate the Installation”
notes.evidence: Run the following command to validate that your cluster has proper network connectivity:

notes.front: `helm install cilium oci://quay.io/cilium/charts/cilium --version v1.20.2 --namespace kube-system` fails with "chart not found". What is the likeliest cause?
notes.back: D: the version has a "v" prefix; Helm needs `1.20.2`.
notes.choices:
A) Helm cannot install from `oci://` references
B) Cilium must be installed with `cilium install` only
C) The namespace does not exist
D) The version has a "v" prefix; Helm needs `1.20.2`
notes.choicesExplained: A: installing from the registry is the recommended method. B: Helm is a supported method. C: the error named is about the chart, and the docs tie it to the version number.
notes.explanation: Helm chart versions carry no "v"; only image tags do.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Installation using Helm”, ““chart not found””
notes.evidence: Double-check your version number. Remember: no “v” prefix for Helm versions.

notes.front: Only the nodes of one hardware pool need a different Cilium setting. Which mechanism is designed for this?
notes.back: B: a CiliumNodeConfig object, followed by deleting the affected pods.
notes.choices:
A) `cilium config set`
B) A CiliumNodeConfig object, followed by deleting the affected pods
C) A second `cilium-config` ConfigMap per node
D) `helm upgrade` with `rollOutCiliumPods=true`
notes.choicesExplained: A: this changes the shared ConfigMap for every node. C: the docs describe one shared ConfigMap, not one per node. D: Helm values also apply cluster-wide.
notes.explanation: CiliumNodeConfig applies configuration to a set of nodes.
notes.evidence: Via CiliumNodeConfig objects Cilium also supports configuration on sets of nodes.

notes.front: An engineer wants to read the arguments that Helm produced for the Cilium agents. Which command shows them?
notes.back: D: `kubectl -n kube-system get configmap cilium-config -o yaml`.
notes.choices:
A) `kubectl get ciliumnodes`
B) `cilium connectivity test`
C) `hubble status`
D) `kubectl -n kube-system get configmap cilium-config -o yaml`
notes.choicesExplained: A: CiliumNode objects hold per-node data such as keys and addresses, not the agents' arguments. B: this runs tests. C: this checks the Hubble API.
notes.explanation: The Helm values are converted into arguments stored in that ConfigMap.
notes.evidence: $ kubectl -n kube-system get configmap cilium-config -o yaml

notes.front: How do `cilium status` and `cilium-dbg status` differ?
notes.back: `cilium status` (Cilium CLI) summarises the whole installation; `cilium-dbg status` runs in one agent pod and details that agent.
notes.explanation: Use the first for an overview and the second when one node's agent misbehaves.
notes.evidence: If a particular Cilium pod is not in running state, the status and health of the agent on that node can be retrieved by running cilium-dbg status in the context of that pod

notes.front: How does changing configuration with `helm upgrade` differ from `cilium config set`?
notes.back: `helm upgrade` applies new Helm values to the installation; `cilium config set` edits single values in `cilium-config`.
notes.explanation: With Helm, setting `rollOutCiliumPods=true` restarts the agent pods gradually; the Cilium CLI route works value by value.
notes.evidence: Via helm upgrade Do so by providing new values to Helm and applying them to the existing installation. By setting the value rollOutCiliumPods=true, the agent pods will be gradually restarted. Via cilium config set The Cilium CLI has the ability to update individual values in the cilium-config ConfigMap.
